title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Stuns With $15 Million Debut, ‘Street Fighter’ Leads With $31 Million
description:
“You Can See Everything” accomplished a true box office feat, becoming the rare must-see documentary on the big screen.

	Director Nathan Fielder a
body:
“You Can See Everything” accomplished a true box office feat, becoming the rare must-see documentary on the big screen.

	Director Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-hyped look at Elizabeth Holmes has generated a massive $15 million from just 855 theaters. Those ticket sales were enough for second place behind another newcomer, Paramount’s video game adaptation “Street Fighter,” which opened to $30 million from 3,575 venues. Heading into the weekend, “You Can See Everything” was aiming for $7 million to $8 million, which would have been remarkable for a documentary, especially one that doesn’t involve music or capture a wildly popular concert. Not to mention, this one runs at nearly three hours and wasn’t on anyone’s radar until two months ago.
	

	After a surprise world premiere at Telluride Film Festival, “You Can See Everything” became a word-of-mouth sensation, bolstered by some of the best reviews of the year. A24, which produced the movie in secret over three years for roughly $7 million, reported more than 2,000 sold-out screenings as audiences rushed to theaters to avoid spoilers on the stranger-than-fiction story about the Theranos founder before she began an 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. Around 70% of opening weekend crowds were under 35 years old, and, according to exit polls, 90% of ticket buyers would “definitely recommend” the film and 80% said it was “even better than expected.” Those reactions signal a long theatrical life for the movie, which is expanding nationwide in the weeks to come.


	“This is a giant weekend for the genre,” says analyst David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “Documentaries rarely receive a wide release — there’s only one every other year — and they average $3 million over their first three days.” 
	

	This year has been an exception with two major docs, the other being Amazon MGM’s “Melania,” a $40-million-budgeted glimpse at first lady Melania Trump. That film opened to $7.1 million from 1,778 theaters — at the time registering as the biggest opening for a non-music or concert doc in over a decade — and ended its run with $16.3 million. (“You Can See Everything” carries a budget in the single digits and will be much more profitable than “Melania.)

	Among its opening weekend bona fides, “You Can See Everything” secured the largest debut for any film playing on under 1,000 screens since 2006’s “Borat,” which ignited to $26 million from 837 theaters (not adjusted for inflation). And it’s the biggest opening for a documentary in over 20 years, since 2004’s seminal “Fahrenheit 9/11,” which premiered to $24 million from 868 theaters (not adjusted for inflation). Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are notable, not just for a documentary, but any arthouse release these days. By comparison, A24’s box office hit “The Drama,” anchored by two of Hollywood’s biggest stars in Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, opened earlier this year to $14.3 million from 3,087 theaters.

	“Street Fighter” collected another $20.1 million overseas for a decent global start of $51.1 million. Critics and audiences were lukewarm on the video game reboot, which landed a “B-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls and a 42% on Rotten Tomatoes. Directed by Kitao Sakurai and starring Noah Centineo and Andrew Koji, “Street Fighter” follows two estranged fighters who are recruited to enter a tournament that forces them to face off against each other.

	Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed “Street Fighter” for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution. The long-gestating film was originally set at Sony as part of Legendary’s pact with the studio and moved to Paramount once the initial deal expired. It’s the third movie based on the Capcom video game series following 1994’s box office winner “Street Fighter,” starring Jean-Claude Van Damme, and 2009’s misfire “Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li.”

	“Whalefall” and “Sense and Sensibility,” two other newcomers, launched in fourth and fifth place, respectively. Disney and 20th Century’s “Whalefall,” a survival thriller starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver who is swallowed by a sperm whale, missed expectations with $8 million from 3,065 locations. Reception were mixed, with audiences bestowing a “B” grade on CinemaScore and critics’ reviews averaging a 71% on Rotten Tomatoes. “Whalefall” cost $60 million and requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales.
	

	“Sense and Sensibility,” the latest remake of Jane Austen’s classic, opened to $7.2 million from 2,545 screens. Led by Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, the Focus Features film carries a $25 million budget and doesn’t have as high a hurdle to get out of the red.

	Neither were able to outperform Universal’s horror film “Other Mommy,” which claimed the No. 3 spot with $8.3 million in its second weekend of release, a painful 70% decline from its debut. “Other Mommy” has grossed $44.8 million domestically against a modest $18 million budget. 

	More to come…

title: James Austin Johnson’s Trump Stops by ‘SNL U.K.’ for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: ‘You Don’t Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?’
description:
Donald Trump made his first appearance on “SNL U.K.,” courtesy of “SNL” cast member James Austin Johnson.

	Saturday night’s cold open recreated U.
body:
Donald Trump made his first appearance on “SNL U.K.,” courtesy of “SNL” cast member James Austin Johnson.

	Saturday night’s cold open recreated U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) meeting with Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy (Freddie Meredith) to reaffirm Britain’s support in their war with Russia. 

	“We need America to restore the Starlink internet. Without it, we are vulnerable to drone strikes,” Meredith’s Zelenskyy said. “Also, it is very difficult to stream ‘Celebrity Traitors.’ I’m very behind, no spoilers, but I think Richard E. Grant is going to go all the way.”
	

	Replied Fouracres as Burnham, “Well, I can promise you now that I’ll raise all of this with President Trump at the first opportunity.”


	Johnson then appeared with his spot-on Trump impression, marking the first crossover between the “SNL U.K.” and “SNL” casts. “Did somebody say Richard E. Grant?” he said.

	“President Trump?!” Fouracres’ Burnham exclaimed.

	“That’s right, you say my name and I appear,” Johnson’s Trump sad. “I got the idea from my very close friend Beetlejuice, the late, great Beetlejuice. It’s one of the two ways I am like him, the other is sex pest — alleged, they can’t prove he did that stuff.” 

	When asked why he’s in the U.K., Johnson as Trump said he’s been in town “to see my favorite comedian” who is “performing live at high court in the role of defendant,” referencing the Russell Brand trial. 

	Johnson’s Trump then explained that he is hoping to do a job swap with Burnham. “I take over the U.K., you take over America,” he said. “I tell ya, that place is a real mess, you’re going to hate it. It’s an awful, awful job. It’s a terrible place full of disgusting people, I don’t know what the hell happened. C’mon, job swap with me!” 
	

	Fouracres as Burnham replied, “I can’t swap jobs with you now, cocker! I’ve barely gotten started. People don’t even hate me yet!” 

	Johnson’s Trump then went on a rant about things he could fix in Britain, including that M&S have too many variations of Percy Pigs. 

	“And how about British comedy, folks? What a bad situation, it’s not doing well,” he continued. “‘SNL U.K.,’ you’re telling me you don’t have a guy — the whole cast, you don’t have one guy who can play Trump? What an awful situation. Some of these people went to RADA! What is that, the Royal Academy of Dogshit Actors? Ooh, you can say shit on this one! That felt really good.” 

	Johnson as Trump finally gave up on the job swap, saying: “Fine, I’ll go home. And Zelenskyy, let me know if you need anything, anything at all. Provided it’s not help with war.”

	Added Fouracres as Burnham, “Sorry Zelenskyy, me old mocker. But as dire as things might be, what matters most is that we all be nice to this insane man.”

title: Inside ‘The New Stanford Prison Experiment,’ Netflix’s Controversial Reality Series: ‘People Are Going to Have Very Strong Feelings’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: It is one of the most notorious social experiments ever conducted, inspiring numerous films, documentaries and psychological studies. In August of 1
body:
It is one of the most notorious social experiments ever conducted, inspiring numerous films, documentaries and psychological studies. In August of 1971, Stanford psychology professor Philip Zimbardo recruited 24 male college students to participate in a study — funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research — about antisocial behavior and the effects of imprisonment. Selected students passed a psych screening and didn’t have criminal records or medical conditions. The psychology department was transformed into a mock prison replete with small cells, a corridor doubling as a prison yard and a closet for “solitary confinement, and for two weeks, at a rate of $15 a day ($124.79 in 2026), participants would be dropped into a simulated prison environment and assigned randomly to the role of prison guard or prisoner. They were referred to only by the number on their prison uniform as a form of dehumanization, and guards were encouraged to maintain order by any means necessary.
	

	By Day 2 of the study, the inmates had staged a rebellion against the guards, using their beds to barricade themselves inside their cells; the guards responded by spraying the prisoners with fire extinguishers, forcing them to strip and sleep on the cold concrete floor. As the situation worsened, with guards exhibiting increasingly cruel forms of punishment and several prisoners suffering mental breakdowns, the Stanford prison experiment was ended on the sixth day. It’s now considered a colossal ethical failure due to its lack of safeguards for participants, neglecting to properly inform partakers of the parameters, poor oversight and the fact that the man conducting the experiment, Dr. Zimbardo, also served as the “prison” superintendent.
	

	So, now would be the perfect time for a redo, right? Right?!



	“The New Stanford Prison Experiment”, debuting Oct. 21 on Netflix, is meant to serve as a cultural corrective of sorts — an attempt to see if the Stanford prison experiment could actually yield valuable insights into the human condition if done correctly. It seeks to answer the question, “Does power corrupt?” And raises additional ones about conformity, dominance/submission, voyeurism and the bounds of reality television.

	Executive produced by Jane Lipsitz and Dan Cutforth (“Top Chef,” “Project Runway”) via their production company Alfred Street Industries, “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” takes thirty participants from diverse backgrounds, transports them to a decommissioned section of a real working prison — the Adult Detention Center in Cherokee County, Georgia — and simulates a prison environment over two weeks, assigning eight as guards (splitting them up between separate day shift and night shift teams) and 22 as prisoners.

	“We were definitely nervous to take on something that has already failed — that is a nerve-wracking place to be — but we felt the question it was asking was very relevant and important today,” Lipsitz tells Variety. “Still, there were moments where we thought it would end on the same day that the original experiment did.” (More on that later.)

	Whereas the original study was comprised of all white male college students (and one Asian American) from similar economic backgrounds, this new iteration features folks of all races and walks of life, including three women. Furthermore, the crew took pains to make sure the inmates or guards weren’t aware of the production, so as not to influence their decision-making, by having no crew members in the pod and everything shot on Robocam.



	

									Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026
	



	The show implemented a number of safeguards to ensure that things never went haywire, including “extensive background checks and psychological testing” for all participants, informed consent, medics and psychologists on call 24/7, a safe word (“pineapple”) if they ever felt they needed to leave or wanted to talk to a therapist and/or producer and a series of confessional interviews throughout the experiment. “The production paid for off-duty guards to be on hand in case anything got out of hand, so there were trained professionals on the spot who could handle anything that went awry,” explains Cutforth, including Major Boughner, who served as commander of both the real side of the correctional facility and the experimental pod.
	

	There was also a panel of experts observing the inmates and guards at all times, and advising production on the ethics of the undertaking: Alison Wood Brooks, a behavioral scientist who teaches a course called “How to talk gooder in business and life” at Harvard Business School; Michael Cantrell, a former federal corrections officer; and Trymaine Lee, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist. And yes, participants in the experiment/reality show were paid, though Lipsitz and Cutforth were unable to disclose just how much.

	“We did not want to pay them enough that they were doing this for the money because then it defeats the purpose of the experiment,” offers Lipsitz. “We were surprised by how many people wanted to do it. There’s no big prize at the end and you’re not meeting the love of your life. I think people wanted to understand what they were capable of and were interested in the concept of power, and what kinds of decisions they would make under these circumstances.”

	“People wanted to challenge their own integrity and morality, and some people just wanted to see if they could stay in there for 14 days and eat prison food,” adds Cutforth.



	

					Dan Cutforth and Jane Lipsitz.
									Getty Images
	



	“The New Stanford Prison Experiment” establishes its uneasy tone early on. Upon entering the prison, the 22 inmates hear loud yelling and heckling through the walls, since there are real prisoners on the other side of them. “That was real,” maintains Lipsitz. “The moment when they were in there and the real inmates started to scream, it really did have a big effect on the people as they came in, and I think it was a contributing factor to some people dropping out,” says Cutforth. “It made them aware that this is not a joke.”

	According to Lipsitz and Cutforth, six people ended up dropping out of the show after it became too intense for them, though not all of these people made the final cut. And unlike the original experiment, the Netflix series allowed those with criminal pasts to participate, such as “Scary” Larry Foy who, by his estimation, had spent over 300 days in jail and tells his cellmate that he’d tried to kill his brother. “Scary” Larry seems to not take well to being back behind bars from the get-go, but the show’s producers insist that everything remained safe. “There were definitely participants who had been to jail,” admits Lipsitz. “But we did very extensive background checks and psychological testing, and Larry had done a lot of recovery work and works as an advocate now for reform. He had changed his life pattern. It was very important to us to not put people into the population who posed a threat.”
	



	

									Courtesy of Netflix. © 2026
	



	Without giving too much away, the experiment takes a dark turn on day six — the same day the original experiment was terminated — as one team of guards quells a potential uprising by imposing a form of punishment seen as extreme by even the other guard shift. Things devolve from there, as the show implements several “interventions,” from asserting the hierarchy to a staggering role-reversal, that drastically alters the dynamic amongst the group. But Lipsitz and Cutforth are adamant that things never got too out of hand. “I would say that it was much more emotionally intense than physically intense,” she states. “There were moments of real concern, but the actual prison guards never had to go in and intercede.”

	Overall, Lipsitz and Cutforth say they’re happy with the way “The New Stanford Prison Experiment” concludes and what the show reveals about its participants.

	“This could have gone a million ways, but I think what it proved is that the question of, ‘Does power corrupt?’ wasn’t actually the right question to be asking,” Lipsitz says. “There were a lot of questions that this answered, but everyone is going to have their own POVs based on their own experiences and we want to leave it up to the viewers to decide.”

	Cutforth concurs: “It’s going to cause conversations and people are going to have very strong feelings.”

title: NFL Introduces Celebrity Guest Cheerleaders: On the Sidelines With Comedian Atsuko Okatsuka and the L.A. Rams (EXCLUSIVE)
description: It’s just before halftime of the Los Angeles Rams’ Monday Night Football matchup with the Buffalo Bills, and comedian Atsuko Okatsuka is standing i
body:
It’s just before halftime of the Los Angeles Rams’ Monday Night Football matchup with the Buffalo Bills, and comedian Atsuko Okatsuka is standing in the tunnel, hyping herself up.

	In less than a minute, the comedian, actress and native Angeleno will strut onto the field at SoFi Stadium to perform with the Rams cheerleaders. Okatsuka hides behind a bright smile while marking her dance moves, but she’ll later admit to being “super nervous.” Sure, she’ll only be dancing for about 45 seconds, but it’s been nearly 20 years since she last shook her poms.
	

	Fortunately, when Okatsuka cartwheels into the center of the formation, muscle memory takes over. Her Venice High School cheer skills come rushing back. (She was voted “Most Spirited,” after all!) The sold-out crowd cheers while the newest Rams cheerleader grooves to the high-tempo beat of Katseye’s “Animal” and, then, in an instant, her big moment is over. When the music ends, Okatsuka strikes her final pose — she crushed it — and now, she runs back toward the tunnel with the rest of her new squad.


	Okatsuka stops to share her instant reaction with Variety: “I’m so old,” she cracks.

	A few minutes later, she sinks into a lounge chair in the green room to reflect on becoming the NFL’s inaugural Celebrity Guest Cheerleader.

	“The middle part I crushed,” Okatsuka says, beaming with pride. “It was so fun. It takes me back to performing good spirits through dance. I haven’t done that in a minute.”



	

					Atsuko Okatsuka during the regular season game against the Buffalo Bills on Monday, Oct. 12, 2026, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Ryan Hadji /Los Angeles Rams)
									Ryan Hadji /Los Angeles Rams
	



	The NFL’s Celebrity Guest Cheerleader initiative is the latest extension of the league’s successful “Celebrity Guest” series, which launched last year with pro athletes, actors and musicians — including Jerry Rice, Simone Biles, Suni Lee, Method Man, Common, Joel McHale, Ken Griffey Jr., Benson Boone and Marshawn Lynch — working as sideline photographers during games.
	

	“Our approach to fan engagement is rooted in finding new ways to bring the NFL into the broader cultural conversation, connecting audiences to the game through the voices, experiences and stories that resonate with them,” says Rob Santini, NFL VP, global culture, social and entertainment.

	“The Celebrity Guest programs are a natural evolution of that strategy: creating opportunities for entertainers and cultural voices to experience the NFL in unexpected ways,” Santini explains. “We couldn’t have asked for better partners than Atsuko and the Los Angeles Rams to bring this to life.”

	The idea for Okatsuka to join the Rams squad came from a popular bit in her 2025 Hulu stand-up comedy special “Father,” where she jokes about how former cheerleaders, like her, are hiding in plain sight. Then, she does a special “roll call” to call them out in the audience. (“Ready?” Okatsuka yells into the mic, as her audience echoes back, “OK!”) The bit continues, breaking down the hype woman mindset that cheerleaders must adopt, pumping up the team even when they have no idea if they’re going to win, and how that positivity manifests in everyday life.

	“We’re always looking for ways to bring the Rams brand to the intersection of sports and culture,” adds Kurt Gies, director, social media and influencers for the Los Angeles Rams. “When the NFL introduced us to Atsuko, we knew it would be a great fit, particularly given her roots in Los Angeles and her background as a former cheerleader.”

	The announcement on the Rams’ Instagram about Okatsuka’s performance generated more than 1 million views. Her performance is one of the team’s top-performing pieces of content this season, with more than 4 million views and 200,000 engagements. “The response reinforced the power of blending sports and culture to connect with new audiences,” Gies says.



	

	



	To prepare for the performance, Okatsuka studied the choreography at home before meeting with the Rams cheerleaders to run the routine at their weekly rehearsals.

	“Stand-up comedy is so different. So, I was like prepping like I’m going to the Olympics or something,” she says. “Once I was there, they were so patient with me. They’re cheerleaders — they’re really good at making you feel good. Not to a fault, but they kept going, ‘You’re doing good,’ and then you start to believe it.”
	

	The Rams also gifted Okatsuka with a customized uniform for game day. “My stylist and I thought about how it might cut for me to have shoulders, kind of like the players,” Okatsuka says, joking about how she wanted to show a little less skin than her squamates. “I was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think I could wear that,’” she says, laughing. “‘Can I be covered neck down?’”

	Okatsuka gets to keep the suit, but she’s not quite sure where she’ll wear it next. It’s a little too much for her next comedy special, which will also shoot at the United Theater in Downtown L.A. “I’ll wear it before, backstage,” she jokes.

	Look for the next Celebrity Guest Cheerleader to take the field during the NFL holiday games. And Okatsuka has a few ideas for who should take part.

	“Shapel Lacey is a stand-up comedian, and he was a competitive cheerleader. It’d be cool to normalize having guys do it. Maybe one of the Backstreet Boys — AJ McLean,” Okatsuka says. “Lil Jon — he was a lot of people’s first cheerleader. At least music-wise, all he does is positive affirmations, so it’d be cool to see him perform with NFL cheerleaders.”

title: Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s ‘Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,’ With Tilda Swinton, Boarded by ‘Triangle of Sadness’ Mexican Co-Producer Piano
description: Piano, the Mexican production and distribution company behind Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or-winning “Triangle of Sadness,” has boarded Apichatpong Wee
body:
Piano, the Mexican production and distribution company behind Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or-winning “Triangle of Sadness,” has boarded Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s “Jengira’s Magnificent Dream,” producer Julio Chavezmontes has confirmed. Tilda Swinton is attached to the project.  

	Just like Östlund’s multi-Oscar-nominated dark comedy, “Jengira’s Magnificent Dream” dovetails with Piano’s ongoing commitment to international collaborations with filmmakers whose work challenges conventional cinematic boundaries.
	

	Weerasethakul’s follow-up to “Memory,” which also starred Tilda Swinton and which Piano co-produced alongside Colombia’s Burning, among others, follows Thai widow Jengira who travels to the ancient rock forest of Sigiriya in central Sri Lanka to scatter her husband’s ashes. Blurred visions distort Jengira’s sense of time and space, drawing her across various time periods. Guided by science and empathy, she becomes a living portal between past, future and spirit. Blending 1970s sci-fi aesthetics with a timeless world where cell phones are the only markers of temporal difference, the film blurs the boundaries between memory, history and the supernatural.


	Joining Swinton are Thailand’s Jenjira Pongpas (“Cemetery of Splendor”) and Sakda Kaewbuadee (“Tropical Malady”) and Canadian actor Connor Jessup (“Falling Skies”).

	In an interview with Variety, Chavezmontes discussed the company’s trajectory over the past 15 years while reflecting on its approach to identifying talent and developing co-productions. He stresses that the company remains open to projects across genres and formats, prioritizing a distinctive creative vision over mainstream formula.
	

	“If something strikes us as potentially incredible, then the format is absolutely secondary,” he says.

	Piano’s international outlook has been central to its growth, says Chavezmontes, whose many credits include Lucrecia Martel’s “Our Land,” Luis Ortega’s San Sebastian Horizons-winning “The Jockey” and Abel Ferrara’s ”Siberia.”

	It participates in the Morelia Film Festival this year – where it’s also throwing a big anniversary party – with Chile’s submission to the Oscars, Manuela Martelli’s “The Meltdown,” which it co-produced, and with five films it distributes: Poh Si Teng’s debut docu feature “American Doctor,” “Mickey,” “The Lost Mariachis,” “Shana” and “Beauty Salon.”

	In the upcoming Ventana Sur, Piano participates in the Proyecta Co-Production Forum with “The Absence,” the debut feature of Mexico’s Jorge Sistos Moreno whose short “The Darkness” debuted at Cannes’ Critics’ Week.

	The company’s approach is built on creative collaboration rather than the pursuit of awards or predictable commercial outcomes,” Chavezmontes asserts. “The secret to our success is very difficult to know,” he says. “But above all, I think it comes down to a genuine belief in cinema and a refusal to approach what we do cynically.”

	Chavezmontes initially established Piano to make his own films, beginning with ‘Halley,” which he wrote and which Sebastían Hofmann directed. The company subsequently expanded into producing projects by other filmmakers, building relationships through international festivals, distribution and co-production partnerships.

	One of its most prominent collaborations emerged through “Time Share” (“Tiempo Compartido”) the film Chavezmontes wrote and produced that competed at the Sundance Film Festival in 2018. The jury, presided by Östlund, awarded it best screenplay. Following further connections with Östlund’s longtime producing partner Erik Hemmendorff and producer Philippe Bober, Piano, which had distributed Östlund’s “The Square” was approached about co-producing “Triangle of Sadness.” “Of course, the answer was an immediate yes!” he recalls.

	The film became the company’s most internationally visible production, but Chavezmontes resists defining Piano by a single title or genre. He points to projects including Mia Hansen-Løve’s “Bergman Island “and “Siberia” as examples of films whose value cannot be measured solely by their immediate reception.
	

	“We tend to be quite chameleonic in the kinds of films we make, and we like to challenge those categories,” he says. “We do that because we’re genuinely committed to exploring new things and finding stories that move us.”

	For Chavezmontes, the key criterion when evaluating a project is whether it resonates with him as a viewer. He describes himself as an ordinary moviegoer and believes that a film capable of moving him can connect with audiences beyond the industry.

	“What matters to me is whether it speaks to me and whether I feel that we can contribute to making it happen, both creatively and in terms of the other aspects of production,” he notes.

	Co-production as a creative engine

	Reflecting on the importance of international co-productions, especially for independent cinema, he says: “Ultimately, what really defines a co-production is the people who come together to collaborate. The creative team, the technical crew – they’re the ones who actually make the films. Money simply makes it possible to hire them.”

	That philosophy informs Piano’s approach to projects that cross national borders. Chavezmontes argued that the exchange of ideas and creative perspectives is at least as important as the financial benefits, particularly when filmmakers seek to realize more ambitious projects.

	Mexico’s next step: a comprehensive film policy

	Chavezmontes also called for Mexico to build on its new 30% tax incentive for both homegrown and international productions by establishing a broader, long-term government policy for the audiovisual sector.

	He welcomed recent initiatives, including state-level incentives in Jalisco and Morelos, but argued that Mexico needs a more comprehensive system of support comparable to those in Spain, Brazil and Colombia.

	“We’ve reached a point where people understand that the audiovisual sector isn’t simply a matter of cultural support,” he points out. “It’s an industrial catalyst.”

	He believes Mexico has the talent, infrastructure, locations and tourism sector to compete more effectively in the international production market. The missing element, he argued, is a stable policy framework that recognizes the economic, cultural and social value of film and audiovisual production.
	

	An independent vision

	Despite the growing scale of international production, Chavezmontes says that Piano’s guiding principle remains its belief in the projects it chooses to support.

	“We make films we genuinely believe in,” he says. “And I think that conviction is what people recognize in us: that there’s an authentic vision behind Piano, rather than a cynical one.”

title: Roger Deakins on Instinct, Experience and Not Knowing What Is a Cinematographer: ‘I Still Can’t Answer That’
description: Walking through Turin with his wife and creative partner James Ellis Deakins, Roger Deakins found himself thinking about Giorgio de Chirico. The It
body:
Walking through Turin with his wife and creative partner James Ellis Deakins, Roger Deakins found himself thinking about Giorgio de Chirico. The Italian painter, one of his favorites, had drawn inspiration from the city’s vast squares, long arcades and unusual arrangements of light and shadow. Deakins was noticing the relationship for himself.

	It’s characteristic of a man who has spent much of his life looking at the world, yet remains somewhat at a loss to explain precisely how he sees it.
	

	“Somebody asked the other day, what is a cinematographer? I mean, I still can’t answer that,” he says.


	It’s an uncommon admission from someone whose images have helped define contemporary cinema, from “No Country for Old Men” to “Blade Runner 2049” and “1917.” But for Deakins, the work is too dependent on the circumstances of a story, and the people telling it, to be reduced to any one method.

	“It’s your emotional reaction to things that’s important,” he says. Technical considerations can be discussed, but the decisions that shape an image ultimately arise from something inexplicable.

	Perhaps his relationship with looking began as something more personal. As a young man, Deakins, born in the southern English resort of Torquay, discovered that the camera offered a kind of confidence, a way of approaching a world in which he hadn’t always felt comfortable.

	“I was kind of hiding behind the camera to a certain degree,” he recalls. “I had confidence because there was something between me and reality.”

	He could scarcely have imagined where that camera would take him. Only in retrospect has he come to appreciate the significance of experiences whose importance wasn’t apparent at the time.
	

	“If you don’t experience things, then what have you got to contribute?”

	It’s a conviction he shares with Ellis Deakins, his wife and essential collaborator on every project since they met on Michael Apted’s “Thunderheart.” For her, experience gives a filmmaker more than a collection of visual references. It provides different ways of understanding the people and specifics of a story.

	“If you’re going to tell a story, having had many different experiences gives you many different points of view,” she says. “You’re able to actually add more to the story.”

	Deakins worries that cinema can become too inward-looking, with filmmakers drawing inspiration primarily from other films.

	“I rarely, if ever, do that,” he says of referencing earlier movies. “You bring all the things that you experienced in your life to something.”

	Their Team Deakins podcast often explores the myriad routes people have taken into filmmaking. There is no repeatable path, just as there is no formula for a good image. James encourages the aspiring to experiment, examine their photographs and footage, and ask themselves why something works or doesn’t. It’s how they develop an eye, or what Roger calls a personal sensibility.

	Deakins, however, is less inclined to analyze his own.

	When asked about the relationship of shapes and forms in his still photography, he struggles to explain what draws him to a composition. He tends to see the whole image, he says, rather than its individual elements.

	Ellis Deakins is more definite. Looking at his photographs, she notices how shapes intersect and contrast.

	“You may not be aware of it, but you are interconnecting shapes,” she tells him. “But I know it’s instinctual.”

	The distinction between conscious intention and instinct becomes more intriguing when we discuss Andrew Dominik’s “The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford.” Much of the film contrasts light and dark, yet the scene depicting Robert Ford’s murder takes place in a bar housed in a tent, surrounded by snow, its interior swathed in flat, even light. The violence, and Casey Affleck’s Robert Ford, seem jarringly exposed.

	Was the contrast deliberate?

	Deakins considers the question. The appearance arose partly from the circumstances of the set: the tent, the snow outside, the whiteness of the surroundings. Whether the scene had been staged there for its visual effect or because of its historical circumstances, he cannot entirely say.
	

	But there were choices to be made. They could have introduced stronger shadows, allowing the light to fall on only part of the tent. Instead, they chose to preserve the evenness of the illumination.

	“I think it was a very conscious decision to have almost a sort of documentary feel about it, as opposed to the rest of the film.”

	He thinks the scene is stronger for it.

	How much is planned varies from one director to the next. With Sam Mendes on “Jarhead,” he worked largely handheld, responding to actors as they performed. With Joel and Ethan Coen, the process was often meticulously planned. Different ways, he suggests, of reaching the same place.

	The common concern is what matters in the scene, and where the audience should be as that part of the story unfolds. For James, that requires entering someone else’s imagination. She recalls her early work as a script supervisor, when understanding what a director wanted meant learning to see through another person’s eyes.

	It is a reminder that, however personal Deakins’ instincts may be, the images are not made in isolation. His way of seeing must always attempt to meet the director’s vision, the actors’ performances and the needs of the film.

	Harrison Ford once described what it feels like to work with Deakins. Discussing “Blade Runner 2049” alongside Ryan Gosling, Ford observed that Deakins’ approach to lighting proceeds from the story, leaving an actor feeling supported.

	It’s a quality Deakins himself describes as the product of collaboration. He particularly misses the intimacy of operating a camera with a director standing beside him, rather than watching from a monitor elsewhere.

	After a take, the director might turn and ask, “How was that for you?”

	“Then there was that sense of trust,” he remembers. He misses, he says, that “intense collaboration and trust.”

	He and Ellis Deakins are careful to distinguish digital technology from the working habits it can encourage. They have always embraced whatever technology best serves the storytelling, and have a long and fruitful history of shooting digitally. But Roger remembers the particular discipline of working on low-budget film productions, when stock and time were precious and rolling the camera was consequential.
	

	“You kind of had to figure out what was the essence of the scene and what was the shot that was going to give you that.”

	Finding the essence of a scene does not always mean moving closer or showing more. Ellis Deakins points out that holding back from an actor can itself create a feeling, leaving the audience uneasy because they want a closer view.

	Deakins recalls admiring Andrei Tarkovsky’s long takes. “They would hold shots, and the shot would become something else. It would be saying something else.”

	He finds another kind of patience in his still photography, where a single image can hold the viewer’s attention indefinitely. And he has spent a lifetime fishing. A couple of days before our conversation, he had been out in his boat off the Devon coast catching mackerel. Enough for supper, anyway.

	“You never know what might happen,” he says, “and you’ve got to sort of change your approach constantly to adapt to the sort of tide and the weather and the way the fish are running.”

	He acknowledges the parallels with filmmaking, without wanting to make too much of them. Both involve waiting, observation and a willingness to respond to the world as it is rather than impose a fixed plan.

	At View Conference in Turin, I later spot the partners attending a number of technical talks themselves. For all their insistence that filmmaking depends on instinct and experience rather than formulas, they remain curious about what others are making and discovering. There is something fitting about seeing Deakins, whose work is so often studied and dissected by others, sitting among the audience, still looking and listening.

	During our conversation, he had recalled a remark by the photographer Raymond Depardon: if he knew how to take a good photograph, every photograph he took would be good.

	I had also mentioned “Moby-Dick,” the novel Deakins chose to take to the island on a recent episode of “Desert Island Discs.” Did he identify more with Ishmael, the observer, or Captain Ahab, the obsessive pursuer?

	“I’m definitely Ahab,” he replied.

	“Isn’t Ahab the captain?” Ellis Deakins asked.

	“Yeah, he goes down with a whale.”

	“A crazy captain,” she said.

	“Searching for something he doesn’t really understand, fighting something he doesn’t really understand,” Deakins replied.
	

	“I’ve always felt an affinity with Ahab for sure.”

title: Ryan Gosling’s Zero-G Stunts on ‘Project Hail Mary’ Broken Down by the Space Epic’s VFX Supervisors
description: For Oscar-winning VFX supervisor Paul Lambert Lambert, of all the huge challenges presented by Ryan Gosling space epic “Project Hail Mary,” the mos
body:
For Oscar-winning VFX supervisor Paul Lambert Lambert, of all the huge challenges presented by Ryan Gosling space epic “Project Hail Mary,” the most daunting was creating convincing zero gravity.

	“Zero-G was probably my personal biggest concern going into the movie,” he said at View Conference in Turin, Italy, drilling down on its VFX.

	“We tried very hard to convince the production to use the vomit comet,” he added, referring to aircraft maneuvers that briefly generate weightlessness. But the spacecraft sets were too elaborate to recreate onboard, so Gosling performed on wire rigs, including a rotating harness.
	

	Removing the wires was only the beginning. When a suspended body still appeared to be hanging rather than floating, VFX artists adjusted the position of Gosling’s legs, arms or torso and added drifting objects to reinforce the illusion. Lambert said the actor was committed to performing his own stunt work, including demanding spacewalk material.


	Other experiments were deliberately hands-on. Fraser used an infrared-modified camera, programmable IR lights and water running in front of the lens to develop some of the film’s stranger imagery. “It was literally a mad science lab,” Lambert recalled. Burning fireballs, liquids, lasers and ferrofluid were also filmed to provide starting points for the microscopic effects.

	The DP returned during postproduction to work with ILM’s Helios virtual-camera system on the sequence near Adrian. Artists tracked Gosling’s on-set performance and recreated it within digital environments, allowing Fraser to choose new camera positions without discarding the original acting.
	

	Across those techniques, the supervisors’ ambition remained consistent: to make even the most elaborate effects obey a recognizable physical logic while ensuring Rocky felt as present beside Gosling as any human scene partner.

	The visual effects team behind “Project Hail Mary” started its journey through space, however, by making an unexpected discovery: much of the sky would look surprisingly familiar. Rather than fill Ryan Gosling’s interstellar adventure with colorful nebulae, Lambert and co-supervisor Mag Sarnowska used astronomical data, practical puppetry and carefully controlled cinematography to keep its science-fiction imagery grounded in reality.

	“We had visions of all these beautiful nebulae, but in the end, the skies were pretty much as we see them today, from Earth,” Lambert told View Conference in Turin on Friday, describing research conducted for directors Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel.

	The team drew on data from the European Space Agency’s Gaia mission to map the stars between Earth and Tau Ceti, some 11.9 light-years away, while studying NASA footage and raw images from the International Space Station to establish how cameras behave in orbit. Exposure became a guiding principle. “If you were to take a movie camera up to space and try to shoot something, you wouldn’t see the stars,” Lambert explained.

	Near the brightly illuminated planet Adrian, background stars were therefore largely absent. Farther from Tau Ceti, where the light was weaker, a hypothetical high-sensitivity camera could reveal them. “Rather than simply choosing when to show stars with dramatic effects, we wanted their visibility to follow the actual lighting and exposure conditions,” Lambert said.

	DP Greig Fraser extended that philosophy into the film’s texture. Digitally captured footage was printed onto Kodak film and scanned back: 5254, with silver retention, for a relatively smooth, subdued Earth, and grainier 5203 for space. Two months of virtual-production exploration before filming also allowed Fraser and the directors to test lighting, camera movements and the scale of spacecraft interiors.

	Rather than dictate final shots, those sessions let the filmmakers experiment with digital environments and camera positions early, with the resulting camera data helping guide the physical shoot and subsequent VFX work.
	

	Rocky, the alien companion performed by James Ortiz and a team of puppeteers, posed a different problem: making a physically present character indistinguishable from his digital counterpart. Sarnowska described three practical versions, including an animatronic and a smaller reference puppet. Framestore scanned the physical creation and studied hours of performance footage, reproducing the puppeteers’ movement when the cramped spaceship sets made practical operation impossible.

	“Our full CG Rocky got really good at mimicking the puppeteers,” Sarnowska said. “In the end, half of the Rocky shots were puppet and the other half CG.” She added that the team sometimes struggled to distinguish the versions during internal reviews. The effects crew also rebuilt Rocky’s transparent xenonite barriers digitally to remove reflections, hide operators and maintain the complicated play of light through the set.

	For Rocky’s sonar-based point of view, the filmmakers also experimented with printing the images onto different film formats, ultimately using 10mm and 16mm for selected shots to give them a more organic texture, to bring a larger credibility to a moving tale of interstellar friendship which proved one of this year’s box office hits.

title: Sergei Loznitsa’s ‘Imperium’ Wins Best Film at BFI London Film Festival
description: Sergei Loznitsa’s “Imperium,” which revisits the Soviet Union of the early 1970s through footage shot by Italian cameramen, has won the best film a
body:
Sergei Loznitsa’s “Imperium,” which revisits the Soviet Union of the early 1970s through footage shot by Italian cameramen, has won the best film award at the 70th BFI London Film Festival competition.

	The prizes were unveiled Sunday as the festival drew to a close. The competition jury was led by filmmaker Sam Pollard, whose credits include “MLK/FBI” and “Citizen Ashe,” and also featured “Life of Jorge Luis Borges” filmmaker Mariano Llinás and DDA chief strategy officer Julie La Bassiere.
	

	“The film is richly evocative and emotionally engaging on all levels giving us a visually arresting perspective of life before the Soviet Union was broken apart,” the jury said.


	In the first feature competition, the Sutherland Award went to Thailand’s Oscar submission “9 Temples to Heaven,” the first fiction feature from Sompot Chidgasornpongse. The film reflects on faith, kinship and the passage from life to death. Actor Amir El-Masry (“Giant,” “Limbo”) presided over that jury, joined by “Moonglow” producer Alemberg Ang and sales, distribution and awards strategist Rosa Bosch.

	“An accomplished first feature paving his own path in the well-established tradition of filmmaking in the Southeast Asian region,” the jury said.

	Bertil Nilsson’s “Masc” received a special mention in the same section. The debut tracks Robin, who drifts between short-term jobs and uncertain relationships while looking for somewhere he fits. The jury singled out Nilsson as a fresh British talent with an unusual concept and a funny script.
	

	The Grierson Award for documentary went to Asmahan Bkerat’s feature directorial debut “Concrete Land,” which spends time with several generations of a mixed-race family in Jordan as they resist displacement and hostility. “Santosh” director Sandhya Suri headed the documentary jury, alongside Melbourne International Film Festival senior programmer Kate Fitzpatrick and BAFTA and Emmy-winning producer Andee Ryder.

	“In a noisy and often polemical world it was refreshing, humbling and deeply relevant to see the quiet resilience and dignity of this family in the face of the erasure of their culture and traditions,” the jury said.

	Theo Rollason’s “Queer Edward II,” assembled entirely from archive material, earned a special mention. It goes behind the scenes of Derek Jarman’s “Edward II,” set against the anti-LGBTQIA+ laws Britain passed in the 1980s, and the jury praised it as a portrait of Jarman the artist and Jarman the activist.

	Rahul Roye’s “Aman” won the Short Film Award. The film centers on a trans man who learns he is pregnant the night before his gender-affirming surgery, upending his sense of who he is as a man and as a father. It is streaming free on BFI Player until Oct. 25.

	Writer-producer Helen Simmons (“100 Nights of Hero”) led the shorts jury, which also included comedian Leo Reich and script editor Jack Casey.

	“We were struck by the film’s painterly cinematography, and expansive and assured storytelling, which guided us through the world with care,” the jury said.

	Elizabeth Hobbs’ “Daughters of the Late Colonel,” about two middle-aged sisters left adrift after the death of their domineering father, took a special mention for its inventive visual style.

	Audience voting for the festival’s best feature film and best British discovery prizes closes Oct. 21, with winners to be named later. Last year, Chloé Zhao’s “Hamnet” took the audience prize for best feature, while Yemi Bamiro’s “Black Is Beautiful: The Kwame Brathwaite Story” won British discovery.

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Jab at Shane Gillis: ‘You Stupid F—ing C—’
description: “SNL U.K.” didn’t hold back from criticizing its American counterpart on Saturday night’s Weekend Update, roasting Shane Gillis‘ controversial host
body:
“SNL U.K.” didn’t hold back from criticizing its American counterpart on Saturday night’s Weekend Update, roasting Shane Gillis‘ controversial hosting appearance.

	After cracking jokes about everything from U.S. President Donald Trump’s recently fired press secretary to ridiculous claims that King Charles might be Muslim, co-host Ania Magliano turned her attention to Gillis. The comedian caused quite the stir last weekend for making misogynistic comments in his opening monologue as well as dropping the f-bomb live on air, which is not allowed per NBC guidelines.
	

	“I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now?” Gillis said during his monologue. “You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial bait-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look! You’re not allowed to look.”


	Magliano riffed on this by saying: “A ride operator at Munich Oktoberfest was praised for giving out free cycling shorts to female riders. Wearing the gym shorts will protect women from being upskirted, but it does make them vulnerable to something much worse.”

	A photo of Gillis during his monologue then appeared on screen, sparking laughter from the live audience. 

	Magliano then took aim at Gillis’ accidental f-bomb, subtly pointing out the fact that “SNL U.K.” is allowed to swear on air. 

	“Last week on ‘SNL,’ comedian Shane Gillis also caused controversy by dropping the f-bomb,” she said. “Oh, Shane. You’re not allowed to say that, you stupid fucking cunt.”

body:
Eric Dane Posthumous Memoir
                          Describes Moment Daughter Rescued Him from Drowning
                          During ALS Battle
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 18, 2026
                            7:35 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Eric Dane said one of his scariest moments amid his ALS battle came in the water ... when his daughter had to help save him after he suddenly realized he could no longer swim.
      
    
            The former "Grey's Anatomy" star recounted the terrifying and emotional experience in his upcoming autobiography, "My Book of Days: A Memoir of Moments," revealing how the disease had begun taking away abilities he once took for granted.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            In an exclusive excerpt published by PEOPLE, Dane described being on vacation in Antigua back in 2024, when he got into trouble in the water. His daughter, Georgia, and one of her friends stepped in to help him once he realized he couldn’t swim.
      

            The incident was a devastating wake-up call for Dane, who had to confront just how much ALS was changing his body and limiting his independence.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Dane also recalled calling his estranged wife, Rebecca Gayheart, after the terrifying ordeal ... and said they sobbed together while processing the shocking near-death experience.
      
    
            As we’ve previously reported ... Dane publicly revealed his ALS diagnosis in April 2025, a progressive neurodegenerative disease that affects the nerve cells responsible for controlling voluntary muscles. 
      
    
            Dane died at the age of 53 after his struggle with the debilitating disease. At the time, his family told us “He will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered always. Eric adored his fans and is forever grateful for the outpouring of love and support he’s received.”
      
    
            The actor, best known for playing Dr. Mark Sloan on "Grey's Anatomy" and Cal Jacobs on "Euphoria," subsequently used his platform to raise awareness about the disease.
      
    
            The book is a testament to the family moments that mattered most to Dane as he faced a disease that claimed his everyday abilities until it ultimately claimed his life.

            The incident happened Saturday night inside the Alamodome before the University of Texas at San Antonio’s game against Navy.
      
    
            Four members of the Air Force’s 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2 were scheduled to rappel from the stadium rafters to the field as part of UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game, according to Task & Purpose.
      

            In video posted online, one of the airmen appeared to lose control during the descent and fell hard to the ground.

                          Not-So-Happy Ending to Divorce Drama ...
body:
'Happy Days' Anson Williams
                          Not-So-Happy Ending to Divorce Drama ...
                          Judge Orders $40K to Ex
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 18, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "Happy Days" star Anson Williams is facing some not-so-happy news in court ... a judge has ordered him to cough up more than $40K to his ex-wife over unpaid divorce obligations.
      
    
            According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Anson must pay his ex, Jackie Williams, $40,181.04 ... plus another $7,500 directly to her attorney, bringing the total bill to nearly $48K.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            And he's got a deadline ... the judge ordered Anson to pay everything by 5 PM on November 2.
      

            The money covers several expenses the judge found Anson failed to pay, including nearly $18K in life insurance premiums, roughly $17K in unauthorized use of company funds, and another $2K in payments he made to himself.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The judge also ordered Anson to transfer 160,214 American Express rewards points to Jackie ... so she's getting more than just cash out of this deal.
      
    
            The docs say Anson didn't show up for the October 1 hearing or file a response to Jackie's claims.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Jackie dragged Anson back to court in August, claiming he'd failed to make payments required under their divorce agreement. She also claimed he ignored her attempts to collect the money.
      
    
            The former couple divorced in 2020 after 30 years together ... but clearly, their financial drama didn't end with the marriage.
